findings.title: Barnard's Star slides north across 15 months
findings.body:
Blinking the starlight and 4–5 µm frames in date order, one star keeps shifting up the picture while its neighbours stay put. The ring follows the position I measured in each observation.

That is about 10 arcseconds a year, which matches the star's catalogued proper motion. Worth noting: it is also the brightest thing in the field at both wavelengths, so the centroid is very clean.

Could someone repeat this with a different pair of colours? I would like to see whether the shift is the same everywhere.
findings.author: Dr. Maya Rao

comments.author: Jordan Kim
comments.body: Repeated it with Starlight and Helium: same direction, same size. The older Visible-light picture also puts it well south of this position, which fits.

comments.author: Alex Rivera
comments.body: Neighbouring stars stay within a fraction of a pixel across all twelve dates, so this is not a pointing drift.

comments.author: Dr. Maya Rao
comments.body: Thanks both. Marking this one as explained: SIMBAD lists the same motion.

findings.title: An elongated smudge north-west of the star: galaxy or blend?
findings.body:
There is a soft, stretched source that does not sharpen like the stars around it, and it does not move. In the 4–5 µm frames it keeps a bright core, which an unresolved blend of two stars usually would not.

The brightness plot has a small bump near 3.3 µm. Is that enough to say it is a galaxy, or is it noise?
findings.author: Jordan Kim

comments.author: Alex Rivera
comments.body: Only a handful of samples sit near 3.3 µm and they come from different dates, so I would not lean on the bump yet.

comments.author: Dr. Maya Rao
comments.body: The shape alone is already suggestive: extended, steady, no motion. I would call it a likely galaxy and look for a catalogue match.

findings.title: The same bright dot in every frame: a detector glitch?
findings.body:
A tiny, sharp dot shows up in every 4–5 µm frame, always in exactly the same spot of the detector, even though the telescope was pointing slightly differently each time.

Real objects should shift relative to the detector grid. Does this look like a hot pixel to you?

findings.title: Hydrogen dips in a hot star's colours
findings.body:
This is one of the bluest stars in the patch. Its spectrum drops slightly near 1.28 and 1.88 µm, right where hydrogen absorbs.

Nothing exotic, but it makes a nice calibration example: a hot star should show these dips and a cool one should not.

findings.title: A steady orange star: what does 4–5 µm tell us?
findings.body:
An ordinary orange star, chosen as a control. It stays fixed on every date and its brightness falls smoothly toward 5 µm with a faint carbon-monoxide dip.

If you are new to this, compare its plot with the one in the Barnard's Star post: same idea, cooler star, deeper dips.
